transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, could you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose it’s work, mostly. I’m an interpreter and translator, and for months now I’ve been noticing the same kind of pattern in the project files. Tiny changes—almost too small to explain without sounding like I’m nitpicking—but they keep happening.

It’s in the translation memory, the timestamps, the way the files line up. Certain subcontractors, and one colleague in particular, seem to be arranging things so it looks like my quality control failed. And I know IT says the audit trail is clean, but that’s sort of the point, isn’t it? If someone knows what they’re doing, it can be made to look clean.

Sorry, I’m probably starting in the middle. It’s just… I’ve worked with language long enough to see patterns. Like when a sentence has been “fixed” but the error introduced is too convenient. Anyway, that’s why I’m here. It feels like the record has been arranged so the blame lands on me.
Aside from these suspicions about your files, have you ever heard voices or sounds that others couldn't hear, or seen things that weren't really there?

No, I don’t think so. Not voices or seeing things, not like that.

I mean, sometimes I’ll hear a notification sound and then check and there’s nothing there, but that happens to everyone, doesn’t it? Especially when you’re staring at files all day and waiting for an email. It’s more… patterns in the work, not voices or images. The details are there in the documents.

Have you noticed any periods where your mood, energy, or need for sleep changed dramatically—like feeling unusually elated, irritable, or needing much less sleep than usual—around the time these suspicions started?

I’m not sure I’d call it dramatic, no. I mean, I’ve been stressed, obviously, and when there’s a deadline I might stay up later going back through files, checking alignment, checking whether the terminology got changed after I approved it.

But unusually elated? No. Irritable… maybe, but who wouldn’t be, if your work was being picked apart in this very specific way? Sleep is just… normal-ish, I think. Sometimes I wake up thinking about a segment or a timestamp, but it’s not like I suddenly don’t need sleep. It’s more that the work follows me home a bit.
Aside from this situation at work, would you say you've generally had a hard time trusting people—friends, family, other colleagues—throughout your life, even before this current issue started?

I don’t know… I wouldn’t say I’ve always been like that, exactly. I mean, I’m careful with people. In my line of work you sort of learn to be careful—one word can change a whole contract, and then everyone suddenly remembers the conversation differently.

But friends, family… I don’t sit around suspecting them of things, if that’s what you mean. Or at least I don’t think so. I’ve had disagreements like anyone. My brother once borrowed a book of mine and returned it with notes in the margins—completely missed the point of the text, actually—but that’s not the same as not trusting him.

So… no, not generally throughout my life. This feels more specific. It’s tied to the work and the files.
How long exactly have you been noticing this pattern of files being altered—has it been going on for weeks, or longer, like several months or more?

Longer than weeks, yes. It’s been… about eleven months now, I think. It started not long after I was put in charge of that new localization project.

At first I thought it was just normal version-control confusion, because with localization you have so many files and languages and little formatting differences—people don’t realize how much can shift just from one export. But then the same kind of changes kept showing up, and… yes, about eleven months.
Are you currently using any medications, recreational drugs, or alcohol, or have you been diagnosed with any medical conditions like thyroid problems or neurological issues?

I don’t think so… I mean, no one’s told me I have thyroid problems or anything neurological. Medications, I’m not on anything regular. I’ll take something over the counter if I have a headache, but that’s not really… I assume you mean prescriptions.

Alcohol, maybe a glass of wine with dinner sometimes, but I’m not a big drinker. Drugs, no. I’ve never really liked feeling out of control that way. Even in college, people would make a whole personality out of it, which always seemed a bit performative to me—like they’d come back from a weekend and narrate it as if it were a film.

So, no, nothing like that that I can think of.

Aside from the stress this situation is causing, are you still able to keep up with your daily responsibilities—like completing work tasks, managing your household, and maintaining relationships—pretty much as usual?

Yes, mostly. I mean, I’m still doing my work—I translate, I keep the team’s workflow moving, I answer emails, all of that. The bills get paid. At home we still have our routines, dinner, errands, the usual things.

It’s not like everything has fallen apart. It’s more that when the file history comes up, or certain coworkers are involved, then I can lose time checking things or thinking through what happened. But outside of that project issue, I’m functioning pretty much as usual.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory belief that colleagues are deliberately altering work files to make her appear at fault, persisting for approximately 11 months (exceeding the 1-month threshold for F22 and far short of requiring another psychotic disorder diagnosis). There are no hallucinations, no negative symptoms, and no evidence of a manic, hypomanic, or major depressive episode co-occurring with the delusion, arguing against a primary mood disorder with psychotic features or schizoaffective disorder. Overall functioning is preserved—she continues to work, manage household responsibilities, and maintain relationships—consistent with the relatively circumscribed impairment typical of delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia, where the delusion is usually more pervasive and accompanied by other psychotic or negative symptoms. She denies a lifelong pattern of pervasive distrust or suspicion of others predating this specific work-related belief, which argues against paranoid personality disorder. No substance use or medical/neurological condition was identified as a cause. The circumscribed, systematized nature of the delusion (specific to a workplace conspiracy) with intact reality testing in other domains is classic for delusional disorder, persecutory type.
